statement: Lecture 7 agenda: designing a distributed cache, and ETL and tiered storage.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Agenda: Designing a distributed cache - ETL and Tiered Storage

statement: Running example: a multi-user blogging application whose data is stored in a transactional database such as MongoDB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Say, we are building a multi-user blogging application in which the data is stored in a Transactional Database like MongoDB

statement: As the application grows the CEO wants detailed reports, stats and dashboards, built by a dedicated insights team that only knows SQL, so the data has to reach a SQL store.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But the insights team only knows SQL

statement: One way to feed analytics: the API sends events into Kafka, workers process them and write into a SQL store (MySQL) that the insights team queries.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: One way would be to send "events" from API in Kafka then process it into worker and put it into some SQL sto[re]

statement: Problem with event pipelines: events carry the context of the application, not the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: events have context of the application

statement: Problem with event pipelines: events might not contain all the data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: events might not contain all the data

statement: Problem with event pipelines: not every change has an event.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: everything might not have an event

statement: Problem with event pipelines: if the change is done but sending the event fails, the two stores become inconsistent.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what if changes done but sending event failed ... consistency

statement: Change Data Capture: instead of relying on events, rely on the source of truth, the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Instead of relying on Events, what if we rely on Source of Truth? our database

statement: CDC pulls the changes happening in the database through its commit log / binlog.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDC pulls the changes happening on the database through its COMMIT-LOG / BIN-LOG

statement: CDC can optionally transform the data and puts it into a 'sink' database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: - optionally transform the data - put it into a "sink" database

statement: CDC tools named on the board: Airbyte and Debezium.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Airbyte Dbezium

statement: You can also build CDC yourself: pick an appropriate sink such as Kafka, SQS or a broker and write your own complex transformations.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can also choose to do it manually or your own way just pick appropriate SINK eg: Kafka, SQS, Broker

statement: With a 'Blogs' table, every insert, update or delete produces one CDC event per changed row/document.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we get one CDC event for every change that happened in the database

statement: CDCs are heavily used to build multi-tiered storage.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDCs are very heavily used in building Multi-Tiered Storage

statement: Multi-tier setup: MySQL (transactional) feeds ElasticSearch (search) and Redshift (analytics) through CDC, and Redshift feeds S3 (backup) through another CDC.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Transactional Search Analytics Backup MySQL ElasticSearch Redshift S3

statement: Homework: implement a quick CDC using Airbyte; it will be used a lot in future system discussions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Implement quick CDC using Airbyte (if you have never used it) we will be using it a lot in future System discussions

statement: Distributed cache requirements: high throughput, low latency, distributed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: High Throughput , low latency, distributed

statement: The cache must support GET, PUT, DEL and TTL.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: GET, PUT, DEL, TTL

statement: Scale is a default requirement.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Scale is default

statement: Single-node design topics: storage, cache full, eviction, communication, concurrency, TTL.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: storage, cache full , eviction, communication, concurrency, ttl

statement: Storage on one node: keys and values in a hash table.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Storage: Key and Value in Hash Table!

statement: Values can be richer types: set, list, Bloom filter, HyperLogLog.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: set, list, bf, hll

statement: Commands map to types: 'add' works on a set, 'push' on a list.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: add -> set push -> list

statement: The value is stored as a generic Object / void* plus a type field: MyValue { value *void/Object; type int4 }.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: key -> MyValue { value * void/Object type int4 }

statement: If values keep filling the heap the process hits a segmentation fault, so memory usage must be capped.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Seg Fault ... Cap the memory usage

statement: Tracking memory: a size function, and accounting on malloc / free.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Size function ... malloc ( int size_alloc ) free

statement: Wrap malloc as zmalloc: if total_size + b exceeds the max, trigger eviction; otherwise o = malloc(b), total_size += b, return o (with zfree for frees).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: zmalloc ( int b ) { if total_size + b > max... o = malloc (b) total_size += b return o }

statement: Example memory cap on total_size: 1GB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: total_size 1GB

statement: Eviction strategies listed: LRU, LFU, Random; a priority queue is one way to pick the victim.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Eviction LRU LFU Random ... Priority Queue

statement: The value struct carries an lru_bits field (28 bits) for eviction bookkeeping.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: lru_bits 28

statement: LRU as a doubly linked list: each node holds next, prev and value pointers of 4 bytes each, 12 bytes per key.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: next * 4B prev * 4B value * 4B 12B

statement: For a key 'a' (1 byte) with value 2 (4 bytes), 5 bytes of data carry 12 bytes of list overhead.
speaker: teacher

statement: LRU suits news-like access (a spike that decays); LFU suits Wikipedia-like access (steady, rising popularity).
detail: Recap page adds CDN and Google News as LRU examples.
topic: distributed cache > eviction > lru vs lfu
speaker: teacher
verbatim: LRU ... News LFU ... Wikipedia

statement: Communication between API and cache runs over TCP; options are HTTP/1.1, gRPC or a custom protocol.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: TCP http1.1 gRPC custom

statement: Written '3/2' beside the TCP connection: per audio the TCP 3-way handshake and 2-way teardown paid per HTTP/1.1 connection.
speaker: teacher
flags: check: '3/2' is cut at the page edge; meaning from audio around 01:21:40

statement: Screen share of the teacher's blog post 'HTTP Requests using Netcat': an HTTP request is plain text sent over a TCP connection (netcat localhost 3000, GET /hello HTTP/1.1 returns 200 OK; 'This is a sample' returns 400).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The HTTP Communication happens over a TCP Connection.

statement: Bare minimum functionality of a single-node cache: GET / PUT / DEL; it can be extended to complex data structures like sets and lists.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Bare minimum functionalities: GET / PUT / DEL You can always extend the functionalities to support compl[ex] data structures like sets, list, etc

statement: Each key has an associated type that determines the functionalities supported; key -> object struct { type, data }.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Each key has an associated type which determines the functionalities supported

statement: The objects are stored in a hash table: key 1 -> Object {type list}, key 2 -> object {type set}.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The objects are stored in a Hash Table key 1 -> Object { type list } key 2 -> object { type set }

statement: Communication is over TCP, either raw TCP, HTTP or gRPC.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Communication: TCP protocol Raw TCP HTTP gRPC

statement: Every protocol has its own pros and cons, but one cache server can support all three by abstracting out the implementation over one shared hash table.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But, we can support all the 3 ways of communication by abstracting out the implementation

statement: When the cache is full, eviction makes place for newer entries.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Cache is full!! Eviction Make place for newer entries

statement: Reading: implementation of constant-time LRU (and LFU, text cut off).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: * Read about implementation of constant time LRU & ...

statement: Detecting a full cache: cap the maximum number of keys in the hash table, or cap the cumulative size of the values inserted (total_size += sizeof(obj), via zmalloc).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Cap on the max number of keys in the cache ... Cap on the cumulative size of the values inserted total_size += sizeof(obj)

statement: You can trigger cache eviction only when you know the cache is full.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can trigger cache eviction only when you know the cache is full

statement: TTL: every key has an associated expiry stored as an absolute time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every key has an associated expiry -> absolute time

statement: Every cache server runs a cleanup process that frees expired keys (free(obj)); the garbage collector then picks them up.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every cache server has a cleaup process running - frees up the expired keys free(obj)

statement: Finding keys to clean up: a priority queue ordered by absolute expiration time; freeing happens at the head.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Priority Queue k2:100 , k7:101 , k9:105 , k3:110 absolute expiration time -> order Free happens here

statement: Priority queue for TTLs: simple and consistent, but needs an additional data structure.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Advantages: Simple, consistent Disadvantage: Need an additional data structure

statement: Redis-style sampling with lazy deletion: sample 20 keys, free the expired ones, repeat until fewer than 25% of the sample are expired.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Sampling [Redis] lazy del^n Sample 20 keys, free the expired ones, repeat until the sample < 25% expired

statement: Scaling a single-node cache is vertical: add more RAM, CPU, network.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Scaling single node cache: Vertical add more RAM, CPU, Network

statement: Core operations: GET k checks the hash table and returns; PUT k,v adds to the hash table; DEL k deletes from the hash table.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: GET k -> check the hash table & return PUT k, v -> add to the hash table DEL k -> delete ...

statement: Concurrency problem: two or more update/delete operations on key k reach a cache server at the same time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when two or more update/delete operations on key k come to a cache server at the same time

statement: Three ways to handle it: pessimistic locking, optimistic locking, single threaded.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: - Pessimistic locking - Optimistic locking - Single threaded

statement: Pessimistic locking: ACQ_LOCK(), DELETE K, REL_LOCK(); with two writers (a=20, a=30 on a=10) one waits for the other to finish.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ACQ_LOCK() DELETE K REL_LOCK() one waits for other to fini[sh]

statement: Pessimistic locks are implemented with mutexes and semaphores, and atomic variables to keep track of locks.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: How to implement? Mutex & Semaphore Atomic variables to keep track of locks

statement: Optimistic locking: make updates conditional (update a=20 where a=10, update a=30 where a=10); only one succeeds; implemented with compare-and-swap, e.g. CAS(a, 20, 10) and CAS(a, 30, 10).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Idea: Make updates conditional Implementation: Compare and Swap CAS ( a, 20, 10 )

statement: Fun exercise: how would you use MySQL as a cache server with the same throughput as any other cache?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Fun exercise: How would you use MySQL as a cache server? Same throughput as any other cache!

statement: Why make the cache distributed: one node is not enough to handle the load.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's make our cache distributed why? One node not enough to handle the load

statement: Distributed design topics: storage, routing, availability, reliability, scaling.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: storage, routing, availability, reliability, scaling

statement: Key space split across nodes: (a,j) on c1, (k,t) on c2, (u,z) on c3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: c1 (a,j) c2 (k,t) c3 (u,z)

statement: A routing table maps key ranges to nodes; it can live in a separate routing layer or be held by the client itself.
detail: Board first draws a Routing box with the table, then moves the table under the Client.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: (a,j) -> c1 (k,t) -> c2 (u,z) -> c3 Table

statement: Four ways of routing a request to a node: through a proxy, a smart client talking directly to the node, any node forwarding the request, or a node redirecting the client to the right node.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Cache ... Cache ... IPFS ... Cache (Redis)

statement: Labels on the four ways: node-to-node forwarding is how IPFS works and is NOT used for a cache; redirect is how DNS works; Redis uses the redirect style.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: IPFS NOT DNS Cache (Redis)

statement: A distributed cache is multiple single cache servers working together as a single coherent cache, e.g. behind a proxy.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Distributed cache : Multiple single cache servers working together as a single coherent cache

statement: Hash-based routing: node index i = hash(key) % 3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Hash-based routing i = hash(key) % 3

statement: Range-based routing: each cache owns a key range (cache 1: a-j, cache 2: j-p as written, cache 3: q-z).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Range-based routing cache 1: [a - j] cache 2: [j - p] cache 3: [q - z]
flags: check: 'cache 2: [j - p]' as written; likely meant k-p

statement: Issue with hash-mod routing: going from h = f(n) % 2 to three caches moves K2, K5 and K6 out of six keys, 50% data movement.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Issues with hash-based routing ... New cache server added : cache 2 ... 50% data movement

statement: Consistent hashing is for determining ownership: nodes and keys sit on a ring and a key is owned by the next node clockwise (K1 at 0 is owned by cache 1 at 3).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Consistent Hashing: For determining ownership ... Key K1 ... Ownership ... cache 1

statement: Adding a server: create cache 5 using data from cache 1, then add it to the ring at position 1; only the keys between 0 and 1 move, minimal data transfer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we create cache 5 using cache 1 and then add it to the ring Minimal Data Transfer

statement: Adding virtual nodes is a bad idea for a stateful application.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Note: adding virtual node is a bad idea for stateful application

statement: Scaling up and down is not simple because it requires reading data from different nodes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: scaling up and down is not simple as it requires us to read data from diff nodes

statement: Removing a server can be a graceful shutdown or an abrupt outage; with consistent hashing it again needs minimal data transfer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Removing a cache server 1. Graceful shut down 2. abrupt outage Minimal Data Transfer

statement: A distributed cache under the covers is a distributed hash table (DHT) that maps values to keys spread across nodes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: A distributed cache under the covers is a D.H.T. which maps values to key spread across nodes.

statement: DHTs are optimised for minimal data movement when nodes are added or removed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: DHTs are optimised for "minimal" data movement when nodes are added or removed

statement: DHTs are used in building distributed file systems, DNS servers, instant messaging and peer-to-peer sharing; IPFS and BitTorrent use DHTs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Distributed File Systems - DNS servers - Instant Messaging - Peer-to-Peer sharing IPFS BitTorrent uses DHTs

statement: Decentralized lookup (Kademlia style): the request goes to the nearest node, which says 'goto 2', and the client then sends the request to node 2; no load balancer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Decentralized request nearest goto (2) No load balancer!!

statement: Pointer: watch the teacher's video on Kademlia.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: watch my video on 'Kademlia'

statement: High availability for a distributed cache: replicas and standby nodes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: High availability: - Replicas (state data) - Standby nodes

statement: Reliability: write-ahead logging.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Reliability: - Write ahead logging
